h: Founded in 1879 by James Fleming beside the River Lour, on a site long linked to a holy well of St Drostan. Today part of Chivas Brothers, it is best known for the cask-strength, sherry-driven A'bunadh.
Built in 1975 by Seagram to feed the Chivas Regal blends. The name is Gaelic for 'milk burn'. Largely automated, it rarely appears as a single malt.
Built in 1972 by Justerini & Brooks to supply the J&B blend. It was first released as a single malt under the name 'The Singleton' in 1986. Now owned by Diageo.
Founded in 1895 by Alexander Edward on farmland outside Keith. Its fruity, grassy spirit is a key part of the Dewar's blends, and it is now owned by Bacardi.
Opened in 2014 in a converted Victorian farm steading on the Ballindalloch Castle estate, home of the Macpherson-Grant family. It uses barley grown on the estate.
Licensed in 1824 by James McGregor, a former smuggler, shortly after the 1823 Excise Act made legal distilling attractive. Set in the Haughs of Cromdale, it is owned by Inver House.

Founded in 1892 by William Grant next to his Glenfiddich distillery, partly using second-hand equipment from other distilleries. It still runs its own floor maltings and employs a cooperage and coppersmith on site.
Founded in 1898 by John Duff, who also built Longmorn next door. It was mothballed in 1900, reopened in 1965 and has been under Brown-Forman ownership since 2016.
Set on the slopes of Ben Rinnes, the distillery began as Lyne of Ruthrie in 1826. It was long run with partial triple distillation, which gives a meaty, robust style. Owned by Diageo.
Founded in 1898 and closed by 1983. Gordon & MacPhail bought it in 1993, and it reopened in 1998 with the opening performed by Prince Charles. One of Speyside's smallest distilleries.
Built in 1973 by Chivas Brothers (then Seagram) in the hills above Glenlivet. It was originally called Braes of Glenlivet and is mainly used in blends.
A new distillery in the remote Cabrach uplands, tied to local efforts to revive a glen once famed for its smuggling-era whisky. Opened in 2024.
A newer Speyside distillery near Grantown-on-Spey, opened in 2022. Details are limited as it is still young.
Started in 1824 as a farm distillery by John Cumming. His wife Helen later ran and expanded it, and she sold it to John Walker & Sons in 1893. Now a Johnnie Walker home malt with Diageo.
Founded in 1869 by John Smith, who picked the site for its access to the new Speyside railway. One of Diageo's six Classic Malts.
Founded in 1891 by Alexander Edward and Peter Mackie of White Horse fame. Known for a meaty, sulphury new make thanks to worm tubs. Owned by Bacardi.
Founded in 1852 by William Mackenzie in the Carron valley. In the 1880s it was one of the largest distilleries in the Highlands and even had its own railway. Owned by Diageo.
Built by Chivas Brothers in 2015 on the site of the Imperial distillery, which closed in 1998 and was demolished in 2013. A large, modern plant making spirit for blends.
Founded in 1895 in Dufftown, a town famous for its distilleries ('Rome was built on seven hills, Dufftown stands on seven stills'). Owned by Diageo and used in the Bell's blend.
A new Moray distillery opened in 2023 near Dunphail, between Forres and Grantown.
Built in 1967 for Mackinlay McPherson and designed by William Delmé-Evans. Bought in 2017 by Billy Walker's team, who have focused on sherry and other wood-finished expressions.
Traces its roots to 1810 as the Kilnflat distillery. Part of Pernod Ricard's Chivas Brothers, it is a core malt of the Ballantine's blends.
Built in 1898 by William Simpson, near the end of the Victorian 'whisky boom'. A very traditional distillery with worm tubs, owned by Diageo.
Licensed in 1836 to Robert Hay and bought by John Grant in 1865. It is still family-owned by the Grants, now in its sixth generation, and is known for sherry-cask whisky.
Built in 1886 by William Grant and his family, first distilling on Christmas Day 1887. Still family owned, it is one of the world's best-selling single malts.
Founded in 1840 by brothers John and James Grant. 'The Major', James Grant's son, created the famous Victorian garden on site. Owned by Campari since 2006.
Built in 1957 on the site of an old corn mill by Chivas (then Seagram). It was a pioneer of triple distillation, closed in 1999 and reopened in 2013.

George Smith took out the first licence in the parish under the 1823 Excise Act and founded Glenlivet in 1824. It became so famous that many others added 'Glenlivet' to their names, until 'The' was legally reserved to it.
Founded in 1876 by John Duff. A Diageo malt used mainly in blends, with a light, grassy character.
Converted from the old West Brewery into a distillery in 1897 and now owned by La Martiniquaise. A pioneer of finishing whisky in other wine and spirit casks.
Founded in 1879 in Rothes. A long-time core of the Cutty Sark blend, known for vintage-dated single malts.
Founded in 1878 as a mill converted by James Stuart. Owned by Diageo, it is mainly used in the J&B blend.
Built in 1897 by James Buchanan and W.P. Lowrie for the Black & White blend. Now owned by Chivas Brothers.
Founded in 1871 by Alexander Wilson near the Moray Firth coast, replacing an earlier distillery at Tochineal. Owned by Diageo, with a distinctively salty, coastal flavour.
Built in 1990 by William Grant & Sons beside Balvenie. For decades it went almost entirely into blends, with only small single malt releases.
Founded in 1898 by John Thompson on the banks of the Spey. Famous for its vintage-dated bottlings and used in J&B. Owned by Diageo.
Built in 1894 by Distillers Company Limited, the first distillery built by that company. Its single malt is sold as anCnoc to avoid confusion with Knockando.
Founded in 1821 by Peter Brown. It has held to a very traditional approach, with an old and new distillery working side by side. Owned by Diageo.
Founded in 1893 by John Duff and highly prized by blenders. Owned by Chivas Brothers, it once had its own branch railway.
Licensed in 1824 as the Elchies distillery, among the first after the 1823 Act. Famed for sherry-cask whisky, it opened a major new distillery and visitor centre in 2018. Owned by Edrington.
Licensed in 1824 near Pluscarden Abbey, whose monks reputedly brewed on the site. Owned by Chivas Brothers.
Opened in 2010 by Diageo as one of the most energy-efficient distilleries in the world. Located on the Moray coast, it is among Scotland's largest malt distilleries.
Built in 1897 by John Hopkins & Co. It was rushed to completion for Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee, and the first spirit ran on Hogmanay. Owned by Inver House.
Built slowly by George Christie, who began in the 1950s and 1960s and saw first spirit in 1990. It stands by the River Tromie in the Cairngorms.
Founded in 1786, it claims to be the oldest operating distillery in the Highlands. It is the home of Chivas Regal, owned by Pernod Ricard.
Converted from a flour mill in 1891, using the same River Isla water source. Owned by Diageo and used in the J&B blend.
Built in 1897 and notable for its Saladin maltings. It was mothballed in 2009 and bought by Ian Macleod Distillers in 2011, which now bottles it as a sherry-cask single malt.
Built in 1966 on the banks of the River Livet in the Glenlivet area. It closed in the 1990s and reopened in 2007. Owned by Whyte & Mackay.
Built in 1964 and known as 'the gentle dram' for its light, soft style. Owned by Angus Dundee Distillers.
Built between 1958 and 1960 by Long John Distillers, with a striking modernist design by architect Sir Albert Richardson. Now owned by Chivas Brothers.

Built in 1896 by John Dewar & Sons, whose founder came from the Aberfeldy area. It is the heart of the Dewar's blends and is now owned by Bacardi, with a visitor centre called Dewar's World of Whisky.
Founded in 1898 by Adam Teacher, son of the founder of Teacher's Highland Cream. Unusually for the Highlands, it makes peated malt. Owned by Beam Suntory.
Founded in 2014 by Adelphi on the Ardnamurchan peninsula, the most westerly point of mainland Britain. The distillery is run on renewable power.

Founded in 2013 by the Stirling brothers on their family farm. They grow their own grain and potatoes on the estate. Started with vodka and gin, with whisky maturing since the first cask was laid down.
Founded in 1790 by John Ross, making it one of Scotland's oldest distilleries. It moved to its present site in 1872 and is owned by Inver House. Known for vintage-dated bottlings.
Founded in 1825 by 'Long John' McDonald, at the foot of Britain's highest mountain. Owned by Nikka of Japan since 1989.
Founded in 1798 by John Stewart and Robert Robertson as the Aldour distillery, in the Perthshire town of Pitlochry. Owned by Diageo and the heart of the Bell's blend.
Founded in 1819 by the Marquess of Stafford as Clynelish and renamed Brora in 1969. It closed in 1983 and was reopened by Diageo in 2021 after a restoration. Famed for old bottlings.
Built in 1967 next to the original 1819 distillery, which then became Brora. Known for a waxy, coastal style and used in Johnnie Walker. Owned by Diageo.
Founded in 1839 by Alexander Matheson and later run by the Mackenzie family. Its stag emblem comes from a legend of the Clan Mackenzie saving King Alexander III from a stag. Owned by Whyte & Mackay.
Founded in 1897 as Strathspey. At about 326 metres above sea level, it is among Scotland's highest distilleries. One of Diageo's Classic Malts.
Opened in 1965 inside a cotton mill designed by Richard Arkwright in 1785, on the River Teith. Powered by its own hydroelectric turbine.
A craft distillery opened in 2017 in the former Dornoch fire station by the Thompson brothers, Phil and Simon.
Founded in 1825 by a group of local farmers. One of Scotland's smallest distilleries, it is run on small, hand-made scale. Owned by Signatory Vintage since 2002.
Licensed in 1824 and one of the oldest licensed distilleries in Scotland. It is unusual for a cooling ring that runs water down the outside of its stills. Owned by Whyte & Mackay.
Founded in 1825 by George Cooper in the Angus town of Brechin. Owned by Angus Dundee Distillers since 2003.
Founded in 1826 by James Allardice, who is credited with the first licence here. It is famous for sherry-cask whisky and is owned by Brown-Forman.
Founded in 1797 in Oldmeldrum, it is one of the most easterly Highland distilleries. Owned by Beam Suntory.
Founded in 1875 by James Moir on the Moray Firth coast. It was mothballed for decades and reopened in 2008. Owned by Brown-Forman.
Founded in 1833 and set right on the Highland Line: the stills are in the Highlands and the maturation warehouses are across the road in the Lowlands. Known for slow distillation and unpeated malt.
Founded in 1843 by William Matheson, using old gin stills. It has the tallest stills in Scotland at about 5 metres. Owned by LVMH.
Founded in 1838 by Thomas Mackenzie on the Black Isle. Owned by Diageo, it also runs large maltings serving other distilleries.
Claims to be Scotland's oldest working distillery, with origins in 1763. It is home to the Famous Grouse Experience and, since 2019, owned by Lalique.
A community-owned craft distillery in Dingwall, funded by crowdfunding and powered entirely by renewable energy. First spirit ran in 2016.
Founded in 1964 on the River Leven just south of Loch Lomond. It is unusual in producing a wide range of styles and both malt and grain whisky on one site.
Built in 1960 on the Moray Firth coast near Banff. Its single malt is sold as Glen Deveron or The Deveron. Owned by John Dewar & Sons.
Founded in 2017 by Annabel Thomas on the remote Morvern peninsula. It is an organic, single-estate distillery that is run with a strong focus on sustainability.
Founded in 1794 by the Stevenson brothers, it stands in the middle of the town and is one of Scotland's smallest. A Diageo Classic Malt.
Founded in 1826 by James Henderson in the herring-fishing town of Wick. Marketed as 'the maritime malt'. Owned by Inver House.
Founded in 1812 by Captain William Fraser. In 1835 it became the first distillery to receive a royal warrant, from King William IV. Owned by Bacardi.
Founded in 1845 by John Begg, close to Balmoral Castle. Queen Victoria visited in 1848, and it was granted a royal warrant. Owned by Diageo.
Opened in 2013 as a small craft distillery in Perthshire, known for using unusually small stills.
Founded in 1817 by Hugh Munro in Alness. Owned by Diageo and used in Johnnie Walker.
Founded in 1897. At its height in the 1970s it was the biggest in Scotland, with 23 stills. In 1985 it became the first Scottish distillery bought by a Japanese company.
Built in 1949 by William Delmé-Evans in Blackford, on the site of an old brewery that was known for its spring water. It reopened in 2003 after a period of closure.
A new craft distillery in the Inverness area, opened in 2023. The name is Gaelic for 'monster'.

The original Wolfburn operated in the 1820s but vanished from record by about 1870. The distillery was revived and began distilling again in 2013, as one of the most northerly on the Scottish mainland.
A craft distillery at the far north-eastern tip of mainland Scotland, opened in 2022.
A newer distillery in Easter Ross near Fearn, opened in 2022.
A small craft distillery near Banchory on Deeside, opened in 2021.
A small craft distillery in Perthshire, opened in 2017.
Built by William Grant & Sons next to its Girvan grain distillery and opened in 2007. It makes a heavily peated Lowland malt with an experimental, high-tech approach.
Founded in 1836 by George Donald, it closed in 1918 and lay derelict for most of a century. It was restored and reopened in 2014 by David Thomson and Teresa Church.
A new distillery on the Ardgowan estate at Inverkip, overlooking the Firth of Clyde.
Founded in 1823 on the edge of Glasgow, it is famous for triple distillation. The distillery was damaged in the Clydebank Blitz of 1941. Owned by Suntory.
Founded in 1817 by Thomas and John McClelland on the River Bladnoch, it is Scotland's most southerly distillery. After closure in 2014 it was bought and revived by David Prior, and reopened.
Opened in 2018 in a former tweed mill in Hawick, billed as the Scottish Borders' first legal distillery in nearly two centuries.
Opened in 2017 in the Victorian Pump House at Queen's Dock, on the Clyde. The first new single-malt distillery in Glasgow for around a century.
A farm distillery founded in 2005 by the Cuthbert family, using barley grown on their own land. Releases are very limited.
Opened in 2012 in a former paper mill in Guardbridge near St Andrews, as a combined brewery and distillery. Known for gin and its experimental casks.
Opened in 2015 by Liam Hughes in an industrial unit in Hillington. Its single malt is sold as 1770 Glasgow, named for the year of the city's first documented distillery.
Founded in 1837 by brothers John and George Rate, in farmland outside Edinburgh. One of Diageo's Classic Malts and nicknamed 'the Edinburgh malt'.
Opened in 2019 in a Victorian railway goods shed near Holyrood Park. The first single-malt distillery in the city in around a century.
Built by Ian Palmer, who spent decades in the industry. It makes a malt and a rye whisky called RyeLaw from its Fife base.
Opened in 2014 in converted farm buildings by the Wemyss family, close to the Fife coast and a famous golf links.
Built beside the ruins of Lindores Abbey, where the first written record of Scotch whisky ('aqua vitae') was made in 1494 for Friar John Cor. The distillery opened in 2017.
Opened in 2018 on Lochlea Farm in Ayrshire, which was farmed by Robert Burns' family in the 1780s.
A new distillery in the Dumfriesshire town of Moffat, opened in 2023.
Scotland's first vertical distillery, a multi-storey building on Edinburgh's waterfront, opened in 2023.

Established in 1798, with the current site dating from 1840 on the Forth and Clyde Canal. It was closed in 1993 and revived by Ian Macleod Distillers, restarting in 2023. Known for triple distillation.
A craft distillery in Stirling, established in 2015.
Founded in 1824 by John Haig, a pioneer of grain whisky who used a Coffey (continuous) still from the 1830s. Today it is among the largest grain distilleries in the world, owned by Diageo.
Built in 1963 by William Grant & Sons and the first spirit ran in 1964. It makes grain whisky for blends.
Built in 1959 and one of the few grain distilleries in the Highlands. Owned by Whyte & Mackay.
Founded in 1885 by a group of blenders in Edinburgh's Gorgie district, and today owned jointly by Diageo and Edrington.
A modern grain distillery opened in 2010 in West Lothian. Owned by La Martiniquaise.
Founded in 1927 in Glasgow. A large grain distillery, now part of Pernod Ricard's Chivas Brothers.
A newer distillery at Tweedbank in the Scottish Borders.
Founded in 1828 by the Reid family, and in the Mitchell family since 1837. It malts its own barley, distils and bottles all on one site. Known for its distinctive 2.5 times distillation.
Founded in 1832 and one of just a few survivors from the 30-plus distilleries that once crowded Campbeltown. Owned by Loch Lomond Group.
Founded in 1872 by William Mitchell. It closed in 1925 and was revived in 2004 by Springbank's owners, making a single malt named Kilkerran.
Licensed in 1815, though illicit distilling here pre-dates that. Famous for heavily peated whisky. It closed in the 1980s, and revived under Glenmorangie's ownership in 1997. Now owned by LVMH.
Founded in 1815 by brothers Donald and Alexander Johnston. Known for a medicinal, peaty style, and it holds a royal warrant. Owned by Beam Suntory.
Founded in 1816 by John Johnston, with roots in earlier illicit distilling. Peter Mackie of White Horse later owned it. One of Diageo's Classic Malts.
Founded in 1825 by Alexander Kerr Mackay. Closed in 1983, it was reopened by Diageo and began distilling again in 2024.
Founded in 1779 by David Simson, it is Islay's oldest legal distillery. Its warehouse No. 1 Vaults sits below sea level on Loch Indaal. Owned by Suntory.
Founded in 1881 by the Harvey brothers. It closed in 1994 and was revived in 2001. Famed for unpeated and also heavily peated whisky. Owned by Rémy Cointreau.
Founded in 1881 on Islay's north-east coast, remote and reached by a purpose-built road. In contrast to its neighbours, its main style is unpeated.
Founded in 1846 by Hector Henderson, overlooking the Sound of Islay and Jura. One of the largest distilleries on Islay, owned by Diageo.
Founded in 2005 by Anthony Wills as Islay's first new distillery in 124 years. A farm distillery that grows some of its own barley.
Built by the Hunter Laing family and opened in 2019 as Islay's ninth distillery, with views across the Sound of Islay.
Founded in 2008 by Mark Tayburn, the first legal distillery on Lewis in around two centuries. The name is Gaelic for 'red river'.
A small distillery on Orkney's east Mainland, opened in 2016.
Opened in 2018 in Kirkwall, and best known for the Kirkjuvagr gin.
Reputedly founded in 1798 by Magnus Eunson, a church officer and smuggler. It is one of Scotland's most northerly distilleries and still malts some of its own barley on a floor. Owned by Edrington.
Founded in 1885 by John Townsend, with views of Scapa Flow. Owned by Chivas Brothers.
Opened in 2015 as 'the social distillery', bringing jobs back to Harris. Its first single malt, The Hearach, was released in 2020.
Originally licensed in 1810, with the present distillery from the 1960s. George Orwell wrote much of Nineteen Eighty-Four on Jura. Owned by Whyte & Mackay.
Opened in 2019 by Isle of Arran Distillers on the south of the island, making a peated Arran style.
Opened in 1995 as the first legal distillery on Arran in around 160 years. It sits at the foot of the hills in Lochranza on the island's north.
Opened in 2017 in Borodale House by R&B Distillers, on an island off Skye.
One of Britain's most northerly distilleries, in Unst in Shetland. Best known for Shetland Reel gin.
Founded in 1830 by Hugh and Kenneth MacAskill on the shore of Loch Harport. Known for a peppery, maritime style, and part of Diageo's Classic Malts.
A small distillery on the Inner Hebridean island of Tiree, known for Reef gin.
Founded in 1798 by John Sinclair, and the only distillery on Mull. It makes both unpeated Tobermory and peated Ledaig.
Opened in 2017 in the Sleat peninsula by Mossburn Distillers, in restored farm buildings. The second distillery on Skye.
